title: Why Are My Periods Irregular?
seoTitle: Why are my periods irregular? When to check
description: Irregular periods may reflect life stage, contraception or health conditions. See FIGO ranges, what to track, and when NHS advice says to seek review.
directAnswer: Periods can become irregular for many reasons, including pregnancy, contraception changes, breastfeeding, stress, sleep disruption, weight or training shifts, PCOS (now also called PMOS), thyroid problems, the menopause transition and other health conditions. One unusual cycle may settle on its own, but a persistent change from your usual pattern needs context rather than a single label from a search result. A pregnancy test when pregnancy is possible, a dated cycle record, and timely review for bleeding between periods, after sex or very heavy flow are practical next steps.

sections.heading: What counts as a change from your usual pattern?
paragraphs: A menstrual cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. FIGO’s 2018 System 1 describes normal frequency as cycles every 24–38 days, with regularity judged by how much the shortest and longest cycles differ (about 7–9 days’ variation depending on age). UK NHS advice uses a simpler public definition: periods are often called irregular if the gap is less than 21 days or more than 35 days, and notes that irregularity is more common soon after periods start and when approaching menopause.

Some variation is expected across life, and a single late or early bleed does not automatically mean illness. The useful question is whether timing, flow, duration or associated symptoms have shifted from your own baseline, and whether that shift is recurring. Comparing yourself only to a friend’s “perfect twenty-eight days” often creates noise rather than clarity.

First consider pregnancy if it is possible, even when you think the chance is small. Also note recent contraception starts, stops or missed pills; breastfeeding; approaching menopause; major illness; night-shift work; emotional strain; eating changes; or a sharp increase in training. Stress can influence cycles, but it should not close the assessment before other causes are considered.

sections.heading: Life stages, contraception and other common explanations
paragraphs: Age and life stage change how irregularity is interpreted. Cycles in the first years after menarche are often unsettled while the reproductive axis matures. After birth and during breastfeeding, bleeds may be delayed or unpredictable. In the perimenopause years (often between about 45 and 55 on NHS timing language), irregular or missed periods are common as ovulation becomes less regular.

Hormonal contraception—such as the progestogen-only pill, injection or intrauterine system—can intentionally change bleeding. Ask whether the pattern you are seeing is expected for that method, and record the start date and any recent changes. In India you may also hear “PCOD” used casually; careful assessment still looks at the whole syndrome picture rather than a scan comment alone—see our guide on what PCOS (PMOS) is when that question is on your mind.

Other explanations clinicians weigh include ovulation timing problems, thyroid or prolactin disorders, medicines that affect hormones, rapid weight change, under-fuelling or a sudden jump in workout volume, and structural conditions affecting the uterus. Two people with “irregular periods” may need different next steps even when the surface complaint sounds the same.

sections.heading: Irregular timing is not the same as other bleeding problems
paragraphs: A cycle that simply arrives at variable intervals is a different clinical problem from bleeding between periods, bleeding after sex, or very heavy flow that soaks through protection quickly, lasts many more days than your usual pattern, or leaves you passing large clots. Those patterns need review regardless of whether your calendar gaps look tidy or chaotic.

Prolonged absence of periods also needs a clear plan once pregnancy has been considered. UK NHS advice on missed periods suggests seeing a GP if you have missed your period three times in a row, among other reasons. Thresholds and referral routes can differ by country and clinic; the three-missed-period prompt used here is NHS wording, not an Indian national protocol.

Keep a note of medicines started or stopped in the same window as the cycle change, including short courses taken for acne or colds and products sold for “hormone balance”. That timeline often clarifies the pattern faster than another month of guessing.

sections.heading: What to track, and when to arrange review
paragraphs: For each bleed, record the start and end date, how heavy the flow felt in practical terms, clots if present, pain location and severity, spotting between periods, and associated symptoms such as acne flares, unwanted hair growth, headaches or hot flushes. Add pregnancy-test dates and results, contraception details, medicines and supplements, and major health or life changes. If you are trying to conceive, say so; an app’s predicted fertile window is not proof of ovulation.

UK NHS irregular-periods advice says to speak to a GP if periods are irregular or your normal pattern changes, if periods last longer than seven days, if irregular periods come with other symptoms such as weight change, tiredness or facial hair growth, if you have bleeding between periods, or if irregular periods sit alongside difficulty getting pregnant. Earlier review is also sensible after a medicine change or when pregnancy possibility is unclear.

Bring previous reports if you have them, but do not arrange a broad panel of tests solely from social-media advice. The examination and investigations that are useful depend on the pattern, age and pregnancy possibility. Dr. Charmi Shah can explain what a result changes in the plan and what it does not.

sections.heading: When pain or bleeding needs urgent care
paragraphs: Seek urgent local care for very heavy bleeding with faintness, breathlessness, chest discomfort or severe weakness; bleeding in a confirmed pregnancy that worries you; or sudden severe tummy pain on one side, pain at the tip of the shoulder, collapse, or flooding loss when pregnancy is possible—even if a home test is not yet positive. NHS ectopic-pregnancy advice notes that symptom combinations can matter if you might be pregnant before a positive test, and that sharp intense abdominal pain with dizziness needs emergency assessment.
Those situations need immediate local services or emergency care, not a routine WhatsApp booking. Separating urgent red flags from routine gynaecology review keeps both pathways safer.

If pregnancy is not desired, contraception options can still be discussed while the cause of irregularity is being clarified. If you are planning pregnancy soon, say so at the start of the visit—irregular ovulation changes timing advice and may alter how quickly further evaluation is considered.

faqs.question: Is one late period enough to diagnose a problem?
faqs.answer: Usually not. A single late or early bleed can settle, especially around puberty, after birth, during breastfeeding or near menopause. Persistent change from your baseline, bleeding between periods or after sex, very heavy flow, or repeated missed periods are better reasons to arrange review.

faqs.question: Can stress alone explain months of irregular cycles?
faqs.answer: Stress, poor sleep and travel can influence ovulation timing, but they should not end the conversation. Pregnancy, contraception effects, endocrine conditions and other gynaecological causes still need consideration if irregularity continues or other symptoms appear.

corrections: Replaced anecdote padding with actionable pregnancy-testing, tracking and review advice.
Added FIGO 2018 24–38 day frequency and NHS irregular/missed-period definitions; stated NHS three-missed-period threshold explicitly as the source used.
Separated intermenstrual, postcoital and heavy bleeding from calendar irregularity; urgent pain advice no longer requires a positive test when pregnancy is possible.

sourcesChecked.title: The two FIGO systems for normal and abnormal uterine bleeding symptoms… (2018 revisions)
sourcesChecked.recommendation: Normal menstrual frequency described as predictable cyclic menses every 24–38 days; regularity uses shortest-to-longest variation of about 7–9 days by age band.
sourcesChecked.passage: Predictable cyclic menses every 24–38 days are usually (but not always) associated with ovulation
sourcesChecked.limitations: International nomenclature system; public UK NHS cut-offs (21/35 days) differ and are also cited for patient-facing simplicity.

sourcesChecked.passage: A woman's periods are irregular if the gap between them is less than 21 days or more than 35 days.
sourcesChecked.limitations: UK primary-care advice; Indian access routes and specialist timing may differ.
